content:
Frailty is not a normal or inevitable part of ageing. It means your body has less reserve, so a small illness, fall or change in medicines can knock you back more than expected. Arthritis can push people towards frailty by making it harder to stay active. Regular strength and balance exercise, good nutrition, a medicines review and the right support at home can slow or even reverse it.

What frailty means

Doctors use "frailty" to describe a state, not just an age. Two people of 80 can be very different: one walks to the shops every day, the other struggles to get out of a chair. Frailty sits on a scale from mild to severe, and people can move along it in both directions.

How arthritis and frailty are linked

Arthritis pain and stiffness often lead to doing less. Doing less leads to weaker muscles, poorer balance and lower stamina. That makes activity harder still, and the cycle continues. Other links include:

  • sleep problems and fatigue from pain or inflammation
  • side effects of some medicines, such as drowsiness from stronger painkillers
  • low mood and feeling isolated
  • poor appetite or weight loss, which reduces muscle

Early signs to look out for

  • walking more slowly than you used to
  • needing your arms to push up from a chair
  • feeling exhausted much of the time
  • losing weight without trying
  • falls, or nearly falling
  • doing fewer of the things you enjoy, or going out less

If you notice these in yourself or someone you care for, talk to the GP. Many practices identify frailty and can arrange a review.

Building strength

Muscle can be built at any age. The UK Chief Medical Officers advise older adults to do activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week, and to break up long periods of sitting.

Good starting points:

  • sit to stand from a firm chair, using your arms less over time
  • heel raises while holding the kitchen worktop
  • seated knee straightening to strengthen the front of the thigh
  • wall press-ups for arms and shoulders

Start with a few repetitions and build up slowly. Mild aching that settles within a day is normal. If pain stays worse the next day, do a bit less next time rather than stopping altogether.

Balance and preventing falls

Balance training is one of the best ways to prevent falls. Strength-and-balance programmes, often run by the NHS or local councils, and tai chi are good options. NICE (NG249) recommends that people who have fallen or are at risk are offered a falls assessment and a tailored exercise programme. Ask your GP about local falls prevention services.

Eating to protect muscle

Muscle needs protein and enough overall energy. Include protein at each meal, such as eggs, milk, yoghurt, fish, beans, lentils or meat. If your appetite is poor, smaller meals and nourishing snacks help. Unplanned weight loss should always be mentioned to your GP. Follow NHS advice on vitamin D.

Review your medicines

Taking several medicines increases the risk of dizziness, falls and confusion. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a structured medication review, particularly if you take strong painkillers, sleeping tablets, blood pressure tablets or medicines for mood.

Support to stay independent at home

  • Occupational therapy can suggest equipment and easier ways to do everyday tasks.
  • A council needs assessment is free and can lead to equipment, home adaptations or care support.
  • Personal alarms and good lighting help if you live alone.
  • Benefits such as Attendance Allowance (over State Pension age) are not means-tested.

When to seek help quickly

A sudden drop in your usual abilities, such as new confusion, not being able to get up, or going off your legs over a day or two, can be a sign of infection or another illness. Contact your GP or NHS 111 the same day.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
